reverse_outline.summary: What the reader will learn: twelve failure patterns, their signs, and the design lever behind each
Three key points: failures recur because situations recur, twelve patterns fall under four levers, each started as a sensible choice
Unlike Tolstoy's families, organizations fail in a few shared ways that return after new leaders or charts
Thesis: structural situations draw the same behavior from different people, giving twelve patterns in four lever families
Roadmap of the page: reading guide, four families in order, closing table applied to one incident
The four levers a redesign can change, each family being one lever set wrong
The three scarce capacities (attention, judgment, verification) in which every pattern's cost is counted
The common causal chain: a reasonable lever choice leaves a situation that makes any occupant behave the same way
The four-part layout of every entry / disclosure of what is invented, fictional, credited or the author's own
What a boundary is and the three wrong things that end up setting it
Org Chart as Architecture, signs: reporting lines move but ownership and dependencies stay the same
Why leaders reach for the chart: it is fast, looks fair, and rests on a belief that boxes produce results
Cost of headcount-drawn boundaries: attention lost to handoffs, shown by Corvane's lead time rising from 4 to 19 days
Pointers to the chapters on reporting lines, Conway's law and work-based team boundaries
Overloaded Team, signs: the proven team keeps receiving scope until it is both the best and the slowest
Why overload happens: each small assignment to the reliable team is safe and nobody totals them
Cost of overload: attention runs out and dependents wait, as with Corvane's Core team taking on the rule engine
Pointers to the chapters on cognitive load, team states and team size
Reorg as Strategy, signs: repeated reorganizations with no stated outcome, no review and no transition plan
Why reorganizing becomes a habit: it is visible, quick, unfalsifiable, and can dodge a harder conversation
Cost of serial reorganizations: ownership knowledge is reset and duties get dropped, as in Corvane's two reorganizations
Pointers to the chapters on outcome-led change, running reorganizations and scaling signals

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Interface Patterns: How Work Crosses Between Teams ¶7

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Interface Patterns: How Work Crosses Between Teams ¶12

reverse_outline.summary: Pointers to the chapters on the full case, Conway's law, team APIs and information cadence
What a decision right is and three ways a decision lands away from those who hold the information
Feature Factory, signs: the team builds a requester-driven feature list and controls only the how
Why the factory forms: each revenue-backed request is harder to refuse than to build
Cost of the factory: the team's judgment goes unused and nothing is learned, as when Corvane shipped 41 features and renewals fell
Pointers to the chapters on outcomes, strategy and roadmaps, and empowered teams
Escalation Ladder, signs: teams push routine decisions upward to less-informed seniors and wait
Why the ladder persists: founder habit outlives small size, unwritten authority makes escalating safe, and answered escalations change no policy
Cost of escalation: late decisions by the least informed, from Corvane's Founder Queue to its judgment shortage at 500
Pointers to the chapters on allocating decisions, what each management level keeps, and team authority
Consensus Stall, signs: with no named decider, decisions need everyone's agreement and keep reopening
Why consensus is sought and fails to hold: it feels respectful and safe, but unargued agreement brings no commitment / caveat that trust is a separate matter no decision right supplies
Cost of the stall: diluted judgment and late lowest-objection choices, as in Corvane's open readiness question and Nine-Week Plan
Pointers to the chapters on decision records, planning and the three-function triad
What an incentive is and three visible stand-ins rewarded in place of results
Output Scoreboard, signs: the organization counts what was produced, not customer change, and how this differs from the Feature Factory
Why output gets counted: it is immediate and attributable while outcomes are late and shared
Cost of the scoreboard: no way to tell busy from effective, as with Corvane's hiring wave that met every number
Pointers to the chapters on outcomes of change, product outcomes and measurement
Ladder as Checklist, signs: people pick work for promotion evidence and leave upkeep to others
Why the ladder turns into a checklist: fair written criteria favor demonstrable evidence over cooperative work
Cost of the checklist ladder: cooperation, maintenance and reviewing go undone; no Corvane example
Pointers to the chapters on career ladders, promotion judgment and senior non-project work
Hero Culture, signs: rescuers are thanked and promoted, so the same few people keep rescuing the same systems
Why heroes get rewarded: rescues are visible and deserved thanks, prevention is invisible
Cost of heroism: knowledge concentrated in one person who becomes a single point of failure, as with Corvane's staff engineer
Pointers to the chapters on overload, constraints, incident practice and public praise

results.finding: sections, unit counts and unit forms match the spec

All 66 aligned outline summaries state the controlling idea of their spec paragraph (p01-p66): the lead, the four reading-guide units, the four-part entries of all twelve patterns in spec order, the table and worked incident, the three evidence lists, the checklist and the hand-off. The two callouts are page format and match no paragraph. No summary describes a different idea from its paragraph.

Three units were marked two_ideas; all are the spec's own assignment. How to Read ¶4 (entry layout / provenance) is both clauses of p07's controlling idea ('the same four parts ... and says where its material comes from'). Decision-Right ¶11 (why consensus is sought / trust caveat) is p44 plus its Lencioni evidence, whose 'shows' requires that 'the source's limit is stated'. Checklist ¶1 (four stale answers / eight steps) carries the conclusion's synthesis and so-what before the p65 list, as the page format prescribes. No foreign idea.

Every unit traces to a supporting claim: Introduction and How to Read to S1; Boundary ¶1-13 to S2; Interface ¶1-13 to S3; Decision-Right ¶1-13 to S4; Incentive ¶1-13 to S5; At a Glance ¶1-2 to S1 and S6; What to Take Away and Checklist to S1 and S6. No unit argues something outside the six claims.

Every spec evidence item is present and the draft says what it shows: the Tolstoy quotation (a short shared list, against the quotation), the lever table and its lead-in, Morieux and Tollman with Figure 1 and its caption, each entry's invented line and warning signs, each named source with its point drawn out (e.g. 'The fault, in other words, is in how the interface was built'; 'People deliver what is counted'), each Corvane instance in the cost paragraph, the two declared absences of a Corvane case, and the at-a-glance table with reading instructions and the Launch Queue worked example. The Hero Culture case (p58) is the thinnest: the claim it illustrates is stated in the two sentences before it and the case adds no consequence; judged present and explained, and recorded under flow_is_followable.

All declared transitions are expressed at their boundaries. Sentence transitions: 'The trouble comes back because of where it comes from' (p02, cause_effect); 'Start with the four things the families are named after' (how-to-read, elaboration); 'The levers are what a leader can set. What an organization runs out of is something else' (p05); 'A pattern recurs because of how it is made' (p06); the three family bridges ('Boundaries decide what each team owns. The second lever decides how teams reach across them'; 'Interfaces carry work and information. Decisions need a lever of their own'; 'The first three levers set what people can do. The fourth sets what they have reason to do'); the contrasts between entries ('Where the first pattern redraws lines too easily, the second never redraws one line', 'A gate is an interface every team is forced through. The second interface pattern is one that no team comes to', 'The first two patterns send a decision to the wrong person. The third sends it to no one person at all'); the similarities in the incentive family ('the same substitution in one person's career', 'the smallest in scale'); 'That is the catalogue' (at-a-glance, conclusion_summary). Phrase transitions inside entries are carried by the fixed labels (Why capable people create it / What it costs / Where the book treats it) and in the conclusion by the list labels.

Both flow readers describe the same organising principle as the spec: a catalogue grouped by the four levers in the declared order, a reading guide first (prerequisite order), the table and worked incident after the entries, and a stated small logic inside each family (including large to small in the incentive family). Neither reader marks any section's position as unclear and both say no reordering would help. No lost-thread point is reported by both readers with rating (a) from both, so there is no corroborated flow failure; three single-reader or mixed-rating points are recorded separately as minor.

Reader A (rated a) had to go back two sections to confirm that 'the 19 days' is the figure from the Org Chart as Architecture entry, where the waiting was attributed to headcount-cut boundaries, and was unsure which pattern the number belongs to until the worked incident. The definite reference assumes a figure given under a different pattern and the entry does not say the two patterns share it. Reader B did not report it (B paused only on the 2027-2028 jump in the same paragraph, rated b). The spec assigns the same lead-time figure to p11 and p24; the prose could say so.
results.draft_locus: Interface Patterns: How Work Crosses Between Teams ¶4
results.quote: Corvane calls it the Launch Queue, and most of the 19 days of lead time were spent in it.

results.finding: The paragraph announces 'two more patterns' and names only one. Reader B (rated a) had to go back to the Consensus Stall entry to identify the second and was still unsure it was not the Unowned Interface. Reader A did not report it. The spec's evidence also leaves it as 'an unassigned decision on readiness', but calling it a pattern without its name is the draft's wording.
results.draft_locus: The Twelve Patterns at a Glance ¶2
results.quote: Behind it stood two more patterns: teams cut by headcount, which is the Org Chart as Architecture, and a decision on readiness that belonged to nobody.

results.finding: Both readers stopped at the Hero Culture case, which ends on a bare fact with no rescue, praise or consequence, unlike every other Corvane case. Reader B rated it (a): could not tell how it shows a hero culture and not an overloaded person. Reader A rated it (b): re-read expecting a missed sentence. Because one reader rated (b) it is not a corroborated flow failure. The draft reproduces the spec's evidence 'what' exactly and omits its 'shows' (one person stood between the company and two of its central systems); the ledger fact itself has no consequence, so the thinness originates in the spec's evidence.
results.quote: At Corvane in 2021, with 50 people, Samir Haddad, a staff engineer, was the only engineer who understood both the scheduling engine and the mobile sync.

results.finding: Everything on does_not_know is given before or at first use: the four levers are named and defined in How to Read ¶1 and its table and redefined at each family opening; the three capacities in ¶2; each pattern name with its definition; the sources' terms with a gloss at first use (falling behind, the gatekeeper pattern, the hard approach, adjustment cost, shifting the burden, seeking the wrong goal, rule beating, the Roller Coaster, Hamster Wheel, Bridge to Nowhere, Ivory Tower, Throne Room, Negotiating Table, Counting House, Lencioni's third and fifth dysfunctions); Corvane is glossed as 'the fictional company this book follows' before its first instance, and each named incident is explained in the sentence that names it. Career ladder and team API are defined in place. Both flow readers found no term used before it was explained.

The introduction opens on a specific quotation turned against itself, bridges from the reader's own experience and the previous page, states a disputable thesis and gives a concrete roadmap. No placeholder, restated question, dictionary definition, dawn-of-man or book-report opening.

The conclusion sorts what was argued by how settled it is, gives a synthesis that reframes the twelve patterns as four questions, a so-what, a course of action and a hand-off. It does not open with 'in conclusion', is not a bare rephrasing of the thesis, and introduces no new subtopic: the trust caveat in 'Depends on context' was prepared in the Consensus Stall entry, and the source recap in 'Established' is the page format's evidence label, not new body evidence.

Checklist ¶1 carries the spec's synthesis ('the twelve patterns are four questions that were answered once and never asked again ... Each pattern is what an organization looks like when one of those answers has outlived the situation it was given for') and the so-what ('ask its question again and change that answer, before changing the people caught in it'), followed by the course-of-action takeaway as eight steps.

Checklist ¶2 returns to the hook as the spec declares: 'Tolstoy's sentence was about families. Organizations are unhappy in a small number of shared ways, and you can now name twelve of them and the lever behind each.' It then hands off to corvane-at-five-sizes with the declared relationship (one fictional company in which the patterns appear in turn as it grows from 12 people to about 1,100).

The intro reader predicted all six roadmap promises in order: a section on how to read an entry, then the boundary, interface, decision-right and incentive patterns three each, then one table of all twelve applied once to a single incident, and restated the thesis correctly. The reader's stated unknowns (pattern names, entry parts, whether cases or remedies appear) are not promised by the roadmap.

The cold reader named the Review Bottleneck and traced it to the interface, built as an approval queue through one small team, with verification as the capacity that runs out, and placed the fault in the interface and not in the four people. This matches the expected answer in full.

Each of the twelve entries has a 'Where the book treats it' paragraph naming at least three chapters as links, and the at-a-glance table repeats them. No pattern is presented as a failing of individuals: each 'Why capable people create it' paragraph gives a locally reasonable choice ('Each check is reasonable', 'The impulse is a decent one', 'The gratitude is deserved'), sources are cited as not blaming people ('does not blame the gatekeepers'), and the one case where a person was replaced (the Two Calendars) is shown as the remedy that failed.

Every pattern drawn from a named source credits it in the entry: Build What Matters for the Feature Factory (name and mechanism, fifth dysfunction), the Roller Coaster and Hamster Wheel (Reorg as Strategy), the Bridge to Nowhere and Ivory Tower (Platform Nobody Asked For), the Throne Room (Escalation Ladder), the Negotiating Table (Consensus Stall), the Hamster Wheel and Counting House (Output Scoreboard); Lencioni for the third and fifth dysfunctions (Consensus Stall, Hero Culture); Larson for the four team states and 'falling behind' (Overloaded Team), the gatekeeper pattern, the reorg trigger question and 'Kill your heroes'. The author's extensions are marked as his own, and What to Take Away ¶3 states which names are the author's.
